Good. The kiln was moved after the ventilation work, and I don't want to deliver glazed pieces to a room that no longer handles firings.

turns.text_en: Welcome, everyone. Welcome to the Old Canal Market, where workshops, food stalls and performances occupy former warehouses and a covered yard. We are starting at the southern gate, next to the tram stop. The information kiosk lies immediately ahead, while the central courtyard and the old basin occupy the middle of the site. The site is compact, but the two narrow side lanes are easy to confuse on a crowded afternoon.

We are starting near the main gate beside the southern tram stop. The market follows the shape of old warehouse lanes, which explains why the route is not a perfectly regular grid. The basin once connected traders to the canal, while the southern tram stop is a much more recent feature.
On the plan, begin at the tram-side gate and use the courtyard to locate the craft areas. The lanes are not a square grid.

The weaving shed stands north of the central courtyard, directly beyond the old basin at the end of the central lane. It has working handlooms, so visitors are asked not to enter behind the demonstration rope.

The food demonstration area lies east of the courtyard, where the lane bends towards the canal. It is between the basin to the north and the southern gate. Cooking demonstrations use electric equipment rather than open flames in the old buildings.

The repair tent is west of the courtyard. Turn left into the market lane; the tent is immediately below the historic warehouse lane, before the stone steps. Visitors can bring small domestic items, but electrical repairs are limited to staff with the right qualifications.

Please remember that working craftspeople use these buildings throughout the week. During a demonstration they may close one entrance temporarily, not because the display is secret but because tools need a clear operating area.
The ceramics stall is in the north-west corner, beyond the stone steps along the upper warehouse route. Look for the shaded outdoor tables; the firing demonstration itself takes place elsewhere.

The evening performance stage is at the south-east end. From the courtyard, take the eastward lane, then turn right and continue beyond the covered walkway opposite the visitor kiosk. The stage is closed for technical rehearsals until the afternoon programme ends.
We have located the workshops and performance area. I will now explain how the market’s history affects today’s programme.
The canal shaped this market long before today's craft stalls arrived. We'll look at how the old goods routes connect with the demonstrations and workshops that visitors can see now.
The canal was originally used for transporting grain from the inland farms to the port. It later served many other trades, but that first purpose shaped the width of the basin.
Several historic warehouse doors were made of oak, chosen for its durability under heavy use. The replacement doors are marked, so the public can tell new work from surviving material.

A label on the plan can make two lanes appear close together, although the old stone wall between them means you have to walk around. Use the courtyard as your central reference point when changing direction.
Short craft demonstrations begin every hour during the main visiting period. Individual workshop times are posted at their entrances because some tasks take longer.
There is a public water station beside the central courtyard. You do not need to buy a drink to use it, although the café also sells refreshments.

The heritage volunteers have tried to keep original textures and signs without making accessibility an afterthought. Some routes are longer, but they avoid the steepest steps and provide easier access to the main demonstrations.
Visitors may complete a feedback card at the exit kiosk. The market team uses these to decide which routes need clearer signs next season.
The old warehouse lanes can be difficult to navigate. Follow the accessible route around the stone steps, and check each workshop notice.
Before you leave, check the craft demonstration board; some makers may alter times when a workspace needs to be made safe.

turns.text_en: Before we take recording equipment into the classrooms, let's agree what the study can responsibly measure. Different wall surfaces may affect speech clarity, but they won't by themselves explain teaching quality or exam results. We also need consent procedures that protect the pupils. Which listening conditions could you compare without making claims about individual teachers?
We visited both classrooms and noticed the surfaces were quite different.
The recordings also need a clearer privacy procedure.
What aspect of sound matters most while pupils are working on spoken tasks?
We will measure background noise during tasks, not just how quickly the teacher speaks.
The room sounds different when ventilation is running and when group work begins.
We should measure the classroom environment while pupils are actually carrying out listening tasks.
What about pupils’ names on the recordings; should we keep them?

Families agreed to recordings for analysis, not to having a child's identity attached to a published example. If a name is spoken on the clip, a listener could connect the behaviour to that pupil. We'll use anonymous participant codes instead.
We can use anonymous labels for groups and still identify which acoustic condition was used.
The privacy consent form needs to match what our recording process really stores.
Why is a comparison based on only one classroom risky?
A single classroom comparison is unreliable because room sizes and surfaces differ considerably.
We have to describe those differences rather than attributing every result to one acoustic panel.
We will describe ceiling height and surfaces so we do not attribute every difference to noise alone.
Which classroom task would directly test whether pupils can hear and follow spoken language?
Use a task involving following short spoken instructions, because it depends on hearing the message accurately.
A silent reading task would not directly test the effect of the acoustic conditions.
I can ask the teachers to use equivalent spoken-instruction activities in both rooms.
How should we report the findings without making promises the evidence cannot support?
Present the findings with practical limitations, not as a promise that installing panels will raise exam scores.
Our measures concern audibility under certain conditions, not the full quality of a course.
That will keep the recommendations useful without promising an exam-score improvement.
That settles the broad design. We still need to decide how to check each measurement.
If the ventilation changes before we start measuring, how will we know which background noise we are comparing it with?
Ventilation noise needs a baseline recording before any changes are made.
Otherwise we cannot compare the same room under different settings.
What about microphone positioning—how should we handle that?
Microphone positioning requires a fixed distance from the sound source.
Moving the device between sessions could create an artificial difference.
We still need to deal with student understanding. What would be a workable approach?
Student understanding can be checked with a listening checklist after the short instructions.
This provides a consistent outcome without asking students to make subjective ratings alone.
We also need to consider ethical approval. What safeguard applies?
Ethical approval requires consent documents explaining that participation is voluntary.
Pupils must not feel their classroom grade depends on joining the project.
Finally, how should we report school recommendations?
School recommendations need a cost comparison between low-cost layout changes and more expensive building work.
The research should help staff choose feasible steps, not simply recommend the newest equipment.
Bring the revised observation sheet and anonymisation procedure to the next meeting.
I'll bring the revised classroom observation sheet and privacy plan. We can show precisely what we changed after the first visit.
Agreed. We can discuss the acoustic conditions without making claims about individual teachers.

parts.title: Materials that Help Concrete Repair Small Cracks

turns.text_en: Concrete performs well under compression, but small cracks can develop as temperature, moisture and loads change over time. Engineers have explored materials that might reduce the need for frequent repair. The phrase self-healing concrete sounds dramatic, but we must separate the sealing of a narrow crack from a full recovery of structural strength. Today we will discuss mechanisms, test methods and the limits of current approaches.
The underlying chemistry sounds promising, but repairing a narrow crack is different from restoring the strength of a structure.

The problem begins with very small cracks, not visible fractures. Microcracks are small openings through which water and dissolved substances may enter a concrete element. Their size, depth and connectivity matter; a visible hairline crack is not necessarily equivalent to a deep structural defect.

The central problem is water entering very small cracks. Calcium carbonate can form within certain small cracks and contribute to sealing them under suitable conditions. The reaction depends on moisture and available chemical components. It does not guarantee recovery of every lost mechanical property.

A crack that stops leaking is not necessarily a crack that has recovered its original capacity to carry load. Researchers report these two outcomes separately so that claims remain useful to structural engineers.

Some approaches rely on mineral deposition. Some designs store a healing agent inside tiny capsules distributed through the mixture. When a crack opens a capsule, material may flow into the gap. The capsules must survive mixing without being so strong that a crack cannot release them.

A capsule-based approach works differently. Moisture is needed by many proposed healing methods, either to transport reactants or to support a chemical reaction. An extremely dry environment may limit their effectiveness, while too much flowing water can remove material before it seals.

Materials that perform well in small specimens may behave differently when exposed to variable temperatures and repeated loading. These differences are part of the research question, not merely inconvenient details.

The amount of moisture can change the results of healing tests. Permeability tests can show whether a repaired specimen allows less water to pass through a cracked region. This addresses one practical goal of healing, but does not by itself establish how much load the material can carry.
Sealing a narrow crack in a laboratory specimen is not the same as proving that an exposed bridge will remain safe. Engineers have to measure water penetration and structural performance separately.

Having described several mechanisms, we need to examine the evidence from experiments. Tensile strength must be checked separately when engineers want to know whether a crack has affected structural performance. A specimen can appear sealed at the surface while remaining weaker under certain loading conditions.

Laboratories use permeability tests to assess changes in flow. A control sample without the healing treatment is needed to compare ordinary crack closure with the proposed mechanism. Otherwise a change caused by moisture alone might incorrectly be attributed to the added technology.
A proper comparison includes untreated samples and repeated measurements. Without controls, ordinary mineral deposition could be mistaken for the benefit of a new additive.

The next challenge is whether laboratory success predicts structural strength. Durability is a major challenge because capsules and healing components must remain effective through years of temperature cycles and other stresses. A short laboratory demonstration cannot capture every condition encountered in a bridge or building.

The central problem is water entering very small cracks. Maintenance cost should be included in comparisons rather than focusing solely on the initial price per cubic metre. A more expensive mix might be worthwhile if it reduces inspections and repairs, but that benefit must be demonstrated.
A realistic economic assessment asks whether extra material expense can be offset by fewer repairs over decades. Such savings remain hypothetical until maintenance records support them.

Some approaches rely on mineral deposition. Limited evidence from long-term service conditions is one reason for caution about broad structural claims. Researchers can report promising crack-sealing results without treating a prototype as a ready substitute for conventional safety assessment.

The overall message is that self-healing approaches are a family of material strategies, not one miraculous product. Any claim of success should specify the crack width, exposure conditions, measured property and observation period.
Sealing a crack is not equivalent to proving structural strength. Long-term durability and control samples remain central to the evidence.
